relationships.relationship: Scott argues that Stone’s unequal standards marginalize women’s history and exclude it from defining standards for historical scholarship (1985).
relationships.evidence_note: Scott concedes that his treatment of the two books was generally fair; her criticism concerns his framing and unequal criteria.

relationships.relationship: Replying to Scott, Stone defends reciprocal standards for studying men and women together while apologizing for the tone of his commandments (1985).
relationships.evidence_note: A substantive disagreement within the same exchange, not a second controversy or a denial of Stone’s apology.

relationships.relationship: Scott rejects Palmer’s opposition between discourse and class struggle, arguing that class and gender must be analyzed together rather than chosen as competing priorities (1987).
relationships.evidence_note: Discourse includes institutions and social practices, not words alone. This adds the missing reply direction to the exchange already described in edge_920; it is not a newly discovered second debate. Palmer’s own article was not freshly reread.

relationships.relationship: Scott argues that Thompson’s use of experience makes class identity foundational and obscures the contested construction of gender and other differences (1991).
relationships.evidence_note: She praises his transformative history while disputing its conceptual foundation. Note24 acknowledges Sewell’s different reading. This is Scott’s interpretation, not consensus; Thompson’s books remain unread here. Distinct from the mixed Ranter exchange in edge_511. In her 2024 interview, Scott also credits Thompson’s cultural account of class formation while questioning his treatment of sexual difference in language. This later qualification is separately dated; it does not claim that he ignored culture or retract her earlier critique.

relationships.relationship: Scott credits Thompson’s account of working-class protest as a formative model for making popular action politically intelligible, before her later feminist critique.
relationships.evidence_note: Scott’s 2009 retrospective, p. 35, explicitly names Thompson alongside Tilly. This bounded formative debt does not attribute her later gender analysis to Thompson or cancel her criticism. The 1988 chapter remains unread.

relationships.relationship: Scott recalls Charles Tilly’s SSRC mentorship in social theory, quantitative methods and collective action, while resisting classifications that flattened historical process.
relationships.evidence_note: Primary memoir pp. 33, 35–37, with 2024 interview corroboration. Tilly was her interdisciplinary fellowship mentor; Harvey Goldberg remained her dissertation advisor. Louise Tilly’s separate coauthorship is preserved.

relationships.relationship: Hobsbawm and Scott jointly investigate shoemakers’ radical reputation, distinguishing militant action, left allegiance and worker intellectual life instead of treating the reputation as self-explanatory.
relationships.evidence_note: Substantive opening of their joint “Political Shoemakers” read in the 1984 Worlds of Labour reprint, pp. 103–113, through a third-party transcription. Oxford verifies both authors and the original November 1980 article, pp. 86–114. Collaboration, not a one-way influence; original journal body and the rest of the reprint were not read.

relationships.relationship: Scott credits Hunt, alongside Elisabetta Galeotti, with close readings of the complete Gender and the Politics of History manuscript.
relationships.evidence_note: Scott’s own acknowledgments, printed p.ix, identify manuscript reading. This is a specific editorial contribution, not authorship or a general intellectual genealogy. Galeotti’s joint credit remains. Selected primary frontmatter transcription and its 1988 copyright statement were read; the whole book was not newly read. The host’s 2019 listing is not the original publication date.

relationships.relationship: Hunt singles out Scott’s gender-and-discourse work as an especially forceful methodological example in her case for gender’s centrality to cultural history.
relationships.evidence_note: Hunt’s own introduction, printed pp.18–19 and n.42, places Scott within its methodological framing. This is scholarly reception and use of an exemplary argument, not a claim that Scott generated Hunt’s empirical practice or the whole new cultural history. The cited Scott book was not newly read in full. It is distinct from Hunt’s earlier manuscript-reading contribution.

relationships.relationship: Parr explicitly connects her questions about gender and class categories to Scott’s work on the politics of gender categories, among other named interlocutors.
relationships.evidence_note: Parr’s own introduction to The Gender of Breadwinners, printed p.9, relates the questions posed by her two town studies to Scott and Denise Riley, alongside Mary Poovey and R.W.Connell. This supports a bounded methodological resource, not exclusive derivation or identical conclusions. Selected introduction only; the whole book and cited works were not newly read. Original 1990 publication and later reprints/digital preview remain distinct.

relationships.relationship: Higginbotham places Scott’s language-and-discourse turn among feminist frameworks she found compelling but insufficiently attentive to race.
relationships.evidence_note: Her 2017 retrospective, printed p.632, names Scott’s 1986 article and 1988 book before explaining her qualified dissatisfaction with feminist theory’s racial presumptions. The criticism concerns a wider body of theory, with Scott a named example, not Scott alone. This is Higginbotham’s retrospective account of the context of her 1992 intervention, not evidence of a private exchange, a 1992 direct denunciation or rejection of every Scott argument. James C.Scott’s separate infrapolitics resource is a different person.

relationships.relationship: With Keith Nield, Eley challenges Scott’s portrayal of their approach as a binary choice between discourse and materialist social history, while welcoming her insistence on sexed subjectivities (2000).
relationships.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 83–84 freshly read, with preceding context on p. 82. The reply jointly credits Eley and Nield; this personal route projects their shared intervention, not an independent Eley-only argument. Their praise for Scott’s lucidity, acknowledgment of sexuality’s importance and agreement about Rancière qualify the criticism. Existing mixed debate edge_1169 remains unchanged.

qualification: One guarded old joint-argument route repairs Eley visibility and retains Nield equal credit. New Eley and Palmer replies project already recorded exchanges, not newly discovered separate episodes. Both Thompson debt and critique retain dated own statements. Other old edges, biographies, people and chronology preserved; six source notes append only. No new corpus or life data.
